patterns.name: Dummy / Sentinel Node
patterns.explanation: Insert a dummy node before the head so that head-insertion, head-deletion, and 'return new head' all become uniform operations on a non-null `prev` pointer. Eliminates 90% of linked-list edge-case bugs.
patterns.when_to_use: Whenever you build a new list, merge lists, remove nodes by value, or partition a list. If your code starts with `if (!head) return null;` and then has special handling for the head, use a dummy.
patterns.intuition: The dummy is a never-returned cell whose `next` is the real head. You can splice in front of the 'real' head without changing your code path.
common_pitfalls: Returning the dummy itself instead of `dummy.next`
Forgetting to detach the dummy in languages without GC (memory leak)
Allocating two dummies when one suffices
Using a dummy's `value` field accidentally

patterns.name: In-Place Reversal
patterns.explanation: Reverse a singly linked list (or a segment of it) by walking through and re-pointing each `next` to the previously visited node. Three pointers: `prev, curr, next`.
patterns.when_to_use: Reverse linked list, reverse linked list II (a sub-range), reverse nodes in k-group, palindrome linked list (reverse second half then compare).
patterns.intuition: At each step, save `curr.next` before overwriting it. Keep `prev` lagging behind and advance both pointers. After the loop, `prev` is the new head.
common_pitfalls: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `curr.next` before saving it
Returning `curr` (which is null at the end) instead of `prev`
Off-by-one when reversing a sub-range and forgetting to re-stitch the boundaries
Implementing recursively and blowing the stack on long lists

patterns.name: Fast & Slow Pointer
patterns.explanation: Two pointers traverse the list at different speeds (typically slow advances 1, fast advances 2). When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; if there's a cycle, fast eventually catches slow.
patterns.when_to_use: Finding the middle of a list, detecting a cycle, finding the k-th node from the end (with a fixed gap), splitting a list in half for merge sort.
patterns.intuition: Speed differential creates structural relationships you can exploit. With fast moving at 2× slow, after t steps fast has covered 2t and slow t — so when fast hits the end at length L, slow is at L/2.
common_pitfalls: Bounds checks: must check `fast && fast.next` before advancing fast by 2
Choosing the wrong middle convention (left-middle vs. right-middle of even-length list)
Trying to use fast/slow on doubly linked lists (just go to length/2)
Not handling lists of length 0 or 1

patterns.name: Cycle Detection (Floyd's Tortoise & Hare)
patterns.explanation: Use fast/slow pointers to detect a cycle, then a second-phase walk to find the cycle's start node. Famously O(N) time, O(1) space.
patterns.when_to_use: Linked List Cycle, Linked List Cycle II, Find the Duplicate Number (treat array as a function and cycle-detect).
patterns.intuition: If there's a cycle, fast (2 steps/turn) and slow (1 step/turn) must meet inside the cycle. The distance from head to cycle-start equals the distance from meeting-point to cycle-start (mod cycle length), so resetting one pointer to head and walking both at speed 1 finds the start.
common_pitfalls: Returning the meeting point as the cycle start (it is not, in general)
Not handling the no-cycle case (terminates at null)
Off-by-one in advancement (advance both then check, vs. check then advance)
Using a hash set 'because it's simpler' when constraints demand O(1) space

patterns.name: Merge & Split
patterns.explanation: Merge two sorted lists by repeatedly attaching the smaller head to a result tail; split a list into halves using fast/slow. Building blocks for merge sort on linked lists and for k-way merges.
patterns.when_to_use: Merge Two Sorted Lists, Merge K Sorted Lists, Sort List (merge-sort a linked list in O(N log N) without extra arrays).
patterns.intuition: Linked lists merge with no extra memory because the splice changes only `next` pointers. The dummy-node pattern keeps the merge code uniform.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to attach the remaining tail when one list is exhausted
Sorting by repeatedly inserting (O(N²)) instead of merge-sorting
Mutating one input list and surprising the caller
Using O(N) extra arrays defeating the point
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N + M) merge, O(N log N) sort, O(1) extra

patterns.name: K-th Node & Rearrangement
patterns.explanation: Use a fixed-gap two-pointer technique to find the k-th node from the end in one pass. Generalizes to rearrangements like reorder-list, swap pairs, rotate-by-k.
patterns.when_to_use: Remove N-th node from end, swap nodes in pairs, reorder list (`L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→…`), rotate list, partition list around a value.
patterns.intuition: Move pointer A k steps ahead, then advance both A and B together. When A hits null, B is at the k-th-from-end node. With splice operations, complex rearrangements become bookkeeping.
common_pitfalls: Off-by-one when k is 1 or k equals list length
Forgetting to use a dummy when the head is removed
Re-traversing the list to count length (correct but a lazy O(N) when one pass would do)
Stitching pointers in the wrong order in reorder-list and creating cycles
